questions.question: Q: How did Augustus maintain the appearance of the Republic?

points.text: He kept existing offices and institutions but controlled them behind the scenes. He held consulships, tribunician power and the title princeps (first citizen), presenting himself as restoring the Republic.

questions.question: Q: Why was army loyalty so important?

points.text: The army was the ultimate source of power — emperors who lost military support were overthrown. The Praetorian Guard could assassinate or install emperors. Donatives secured loyalty.

questions.question: Q: How did emperors use propaganda?

points.text: Coins circulated the emperor's image. Statues showed him as youthful and powerful. Buildings like the Ara Pacis linked him to divine favour. Virgil and Horace celebrated his achievements.

questions.question: Q: What was the Pax Romana?

points.text: The period of relative peace across the empire under imperial control. Emperors presented it as their gift, arguing that military power and just governance brought stability justifying their authority.
No formal system existed — each emperor arranged his own succession. Adopted successors could work well, but hereditary succession could produce disaster. Disputed succession led to civil war.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Roman emperors relied heavily on propaganda, but it was one of several essential tools alongside military force and financial provision. Propaganda was pervasive: Augustus's Res Gestae was a masterpiece of self-promotion, coinage circulated his image empire-wide, the Ara Pacis linked his rule to divine favour, Virgil's Aeneid gave him mythological foundation, and the Imperial Cult made loyalty a religious duty. This propaganda provided a narrative justifying imperial power — the emperor brought peace, prosperity and divine favour. However, propaganda alone could not sustain power. The army's loyalty was secured through pay and donatives — no propaganda could save an emperor who lost military support. The grain dole and games kept the populace content more immediately than statues. Bad emperors like Caligula showed propaganda could not overcome incompetence. Propaganda's effectiveness was also limited among the elite who understood the political reality. Overall, propaganda was essential for shaping how imperial power was perceived and legitimised, but it worked alongside and depended upon military, economic and political power. Without the substance, the image was hollow.
